beliefs.practice: Read the cluster connection string (and any username/password) exclusively from environment variables (e.g., DOCUMENTDB_URI) at runtime and never commit secrets to source control; provide a .env.example placeholder instead.

Open the Mongoose/MongoDB connection with recommended driver options: useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true, set a sensible serverSelectionTimeoutMS, socketTimeoutMS, and a maxPoolSize appropriate to the app (e.g., 50) to avoid idle connection exhaustion or excessive connections.
Require TLS/SSL for all client connections (tls=true or tls=true & tlsCAFile as applicable) and verify server certificates to prevent MITM attacks.
Enable retryable writes (retryWrites=true) and idempotent write patterns in the client when supported by the server to reduce error handling complexity for transient failures.
Cap the client's connection pool (maxPoolSize) to a modest number to avoid exhausting server resources or hitting connection throttles, and tune pool size based on expected concurrency and RU limits.

Create single-field and compound indexes on the exact-match fields used by household linking and queries (e.g., normalized_address, normalized_phone, normalized_surname) so equality and group-by operations use indexes instead of collection scans.

Normalize and persist matching keys (lowercase, trimmed, canonicalized address/phone/surname fields) at write time and index those normalized fields instead of relying on runtime string transforms in queries.

Denormalize household data: persist a household document with an array of member _id references and, where needed for fast reads, precompute household-level aggregates (CLV, product counts) instead of computing them on every request.
Avoid frequent cross-collection joins with $lookup for high-traffic paths; prefer embedding or denormalized aggregates for reads that must be low-latency.

Provision and monitor throughput for the sample_customer_360_13 database/collections (RU/s or equivalent), use autoscale where available, and adjust throughput before running large seed or batch jobs to avoid 429 throttling.

When running aggregation pipelines over large datasets, paginate, process in batches, or use incremental map-reduce/ETL jobs; enable allowDiskUse for pipelines that exceed memory limits when supported.

Use hashed or exact-match indexes for commonly-equal-queried identifier fields (phones, customer ids) and create covering indexes for aggregations that do group/sort/limit patterns to minimize RU consumption.
Use TTL indexes for ephemeral/seed/test data collections so sample data automatically expires and does not accumulate indefinitely.

For vector search, create an explicit vector index (e.g., HNSW) on the vector field with tuned parameters and store vectors as consistent typed arrays; filter by metadata with indexed fields before running k-NN to reduce candidates.
Limit vector dimensionality and use float32 arrays; persist dimension metadata and validate vector shape on writes to avoid runtime errors and degraded index performance.

Use multi-document transactions when creating the household document and updating customer documents in a single logical operation to maintain consistency (commit both the household doc and member updates in one transaction).

Implement exponential backoff and proper handling of 429/Retry-After and transient 5xx errors in client code; make operations idempotent when retries are possible (e.g., upserts with deterministic ids).

Use an appropriate write concern (acknowledged writes or w: 'majority' where durability matters) for household creation and membership changes; evaluate performance impact before using majority everywhere.

Enforce schema/field validation either with Mongoose schemas plus MongoDB collection-level JSON Schema validation so documents always contain required linking keys (normalized_address/phone/surname and vector shape).
Use explain() and indexStats to inspect query plans and index usage for the household aggregation endpoints; create missing indexes for any operation that causes COLLSCAN or high RU costs.

Avoid storing very large arrays in a single document (e.g., household.members containing thousands of ids); cap array sizes or represent relationships via referencing sub-collections and page through member lists.

Always project only the fields needed by the client (use .select or projection in find/aggregate stages) and paginate large result sets to reduce RU and network costs for household listing and member queries.
Restrict server access with network controls — IP firewalls, VNet integration or private endpoints — and avoid exposing the database to the public internet where possible.
Keep the sample app confined to a single dedicated database name (sample_customer_360_13) and avoid cross-database operations so permissions and RU accounting remain focused and auditable.

Enable monitoring and alerts (e.g., Azure Monitor metrics for RU consumption, throttling, index usage) and add application-level logging for slow queries and failed link/seed jobs so issues are detected quickly.
